clue.text: Gives an edge to return games ?

indicators.note: to return is to come back, so the word for games is read from its end to its start

parts.note: games are sports

explanation.surface: Someone sharpens their play by going back to games.
explanation.walkthrough: 'return' reads SPORTS backwards. A strop is the leather strap a barber hones a razor on.
explanation.definitionFit: To strop a razor is to hone it on a leather strap, sharpening its blade.

clue.text: Love wet mash Rather un usual

indicators.note: unusual, split by the printer's line break, says the letters appear in an unusual order

parts.note: love is zero in tennis, the letter O

explanation.surface: A soggy mess of affection, rather strange.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition sits between fodder and indicator: O + WET + MASH is rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: Somewhat and rather both mean to some degree, moderately.

clue.text: Lock is to call with rent

parts.note: to ring is to call on the phone
to let is to rent out

explanation.surface: To secure a door, phone and pay the rent.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lock' is a lock of hair, not a fastening.
explanation.definitionFit: A curl of hair is called a lock or tress.

clue.text: Poisonous creature — a blurb writer ?

explanation.surface: A venomous snake is also an advertising copywriter.
explanation.walkthrough: The second definition splits the word as 'puff' (promotional praise) plus 'adder' (one who adds).
explanation.definitionFit: This venomous African snake shares a name with one who adds promotional praise.

clue.text: Decent chap gives us merchandise, or a kind of shirt

parts.note: merchandise means goods
a T-shirt, so the letter T

explanation.surface: A nice man hands over stock, or perhaps a T-shirt.
explanation.definitionFit: A good sort is colloquial British praise for a likeable, reliable person.

clue.text: They may appreciate the usual kind of game in a ship

parts.note: the usual kind is ordinary

indicators.note: in places the animal inside the ship's letters

parts.note: SS is short for steamship
hare is game, hunted for food

explanation.surface: Something might be valued like the regular game kept aboard a vessel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'appreciate' means rise in value, not enjoy.
explanation.definitionFit: Common stock in a company can rise in value, which is what appreciate means for investments.

clue.text: Nickname, even in court?

explanation.surface: A tennis player's nickname means they are level.
explanation.walkthrough: Old Nick is the Devil, and 'the deuce' is another name for him; in tennis, 40-all is called deuce.
explanation.definitionFit: The Devil is called both Old Nick and the deuce, and a tied tennis score of forty-all is deuce.

clue.text: Moor has to put up with a casual greeting

indicators.note: in a down clue, put up means raised, so the little word is read bottom to top

parts.note: hello is a casual greeting

explanation.surface: Someone from a moor must tolerate an informal hi.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Moor' is not a heath but the Moor of Venice in Shakespeare's play.
explanation.definitionFit: Shakespeare's Othello is the Moor of Venice, a North African general.

clue.text: Bird makes complaint

explanation.surface: A bird grumbles.
explanation.definitionFit: A songbird of that name, and a fungal infection of the mouth or genitals.

clue.text: They give many clearer definitions of words

definitions.text: They give many clearer definitions of words

parts.words: They give many clearer definitions of words
parts.note: not dictionaries: spectacles that sharpen the outlines of printed letters

explanation.surface: Dictionaries make many words clearer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'definitions' means sharpness of outline, not word meanings.
explanation.definitionFit: Spectacles for close work sharpen print, making letters more distinct.

clue.text: Someone's meeting a composer in Notts

parts.note: someone is a man, so someone's is man's
John Field, the Irish composer who invented the nocturne

explanation.surface: A person keeps an appointment with a musician in Nottinghamshire.
explanation.walkthrough: 'meeting' just puts the pieces side by side. Notts is short for Nottinghamshire, an English county; the definition means a place in it.
explanation.definitionFit: Mansfield is a market town in Nottinghamshire, so it is a place found in that county.

clue.text: He shows you, me and the lady our places

definitions.text: He shows you, me and the lady our places

parts.note: you and me together are us
a lady is referred to as her

explanation.surface: A theatre attendant leads a couple and a woman to their seats.
explanation.definitionFit: At a wedding or theatre this attendant guides guests to their seats.

clue.text: Water supply, also a Lincolnshire river

parts.note: a well supplies water
and means also, in addition

explanation.surface: A source of water, and a river in eastern England too.
explanation.walkthrough: Lincolnshire is a county on England's east coast.
explanation.definitionFit: The Welland flows through Lincolnshire to the Wash, a river of that county.

clue.text: Eyed rocks ?

parts.note: sewing tools each have an eye, and the same name belongs to the chalk stacks off the Isle of Wight

explanation.surface: Someone stares at some stones.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Eyed' looks like a verb (watched) but describes the thing with an eye for thread; The Needles are chalk rock pillars off the Isle of Wight, an island on England's south coast.
explanation.definitionFit: Sewing spikes have eyes, and a famous group of rocks off southern England bears the same name.

clue.text: Took the part of the billman, in short

parts.note: a parliamentary bill becomes an act once passed
Ed is a short form of a man's name, Edward

explanation.surface: Someone played the role of the soldier armed with a halberd, briefly.
explanation.walkthrough: The page breaks 'bill-man' over a line; a billman is a medieval soldier with a bill (a hooked polearm), but here 'the bill' and 'man' work apart.
explanation.definitionFit: Playing a role on stage is acting it, so took the part means performed.

clue.text: He tells of decay and an island retreat

indicators.note: to retreat is to go backwards, so the whole string of pieces is read in reverse

parts.note: decay is rot
Arran, a Scottish island in the Firth of Clyde

explanation.surface: A man recounts a story of ruin and a remote hideaway.
explanation.walkthrough: 'retreat' turns ROT + ARRAN (ROTARRAN) right round. Arran is an island off Scotland's west coast.
explanation.definitionFit: A storyteller is someone who recounts events, the one who tells the tale.

clue.text: A number go to church in town

parts.note: X is the Roman numeral ten
a minster is a large church

explanation.surface: Many people attend church in a town.
explanation.walkthrough: Axminster is a town in Devon, in south-west England, known for carpets.
explanation.definitionFit: Axminster is a market town in Devon, famous for its carpets.

clue.text: Business man arranges some shooting ?

explanation.surface: A businessman organises some gunfire.
explanation.walkthrough: 'shooting' is filming a movie, not firing guns.
explanation.definitionFit: A board member of a company, and the person who oversees the filming of a movie.

clue.text: Hail-storms the concern of batsmen

parts.note: ave is Latin for hail, a greeting
storms as a verb means rages

explanation.surface: Bad weather worries cricketers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hail-storms' reads as weather but splits into two words: hail as a greeting (AVE) and storms as a verb. Cricket batsmen are judged by their batting averages.
explanation.definitionFit: A batsman's average, runs per dismissal, is the key statistic a cricketer worries over.

clue.text: Ancient attendants have parts in TV's Lear

indicators.note: the letters are parted and rearranged, as actors take parts in a show

parts.note: the letters of TV's, keeping the S

explanation.surface: Old servants get roles in a television King Lear.
explanation.walkthrough: The apostrophe's S counts: TVS + LEAR rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: Varlets were medieval pages or knights' servants, attendants of old.

clue.text: Tribe in whom a saint believed

indicators.note: in tells us the letters lie inside the words that follow

explanation.surface: A people whom a holy figure trusted.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters run across 'whoM A SAInt'; 'believed' completes the surface only.
explanation.definitionFit: The Maasai are a people of Kenya and Tanzania, an East African ethnic group.

clue.text: Conductor was an army man, we hear

indicators.note: we hear means the word is said out loud

parts.note: a sergeant is a non-commissioned army officer

explanation.surface: An orchestra leader once served as a soldier, apparently.
explanation.walkthrough: Sir Malcolm Sargent was a British conductor famous for the Proms, a London concert season.
explanation.definitionFit: Sir Malcolm Sargent was a celebrated English orchestral conductor.

clue.text: Toughen East for record-breaking

indicators.note: breaking means splitting open, so one piece breaks into the other

parts.note: an annal is a record of a year's events

explanation.surface: Strengthen the East so it can beat a record.
explanation.walkthrough: 'record-breaking' looks like setting a new best, but E breaks into ANNAL.
explanation.definitionFit: Annealing heats and slowly cools metal or glass, making it less brittle.

clue.text: Maid in Shakespeare is like a singer retiring

indicators.note: retiring means withdrawing, going back, so the pieces are read backwards

parts.note: as means like
a siren is a singer who lures sailors in Greek myth

explanation.surface: A Shakespearean servant is compared to a shy vocalist.
explanation.walkthrough: 'retiring' looks like 'shy' but reverses AS + SIREN. Nerissa is Portia's waiting-maid in The Merchant of Venice.
explanation.definitionFit: Nerissa is Portia's lady-in-waiting in The Merchant of Venice, a servant in the play.

clue.text: Girl turns up about one with fibre

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so the girl goes round the one
in a down clue, turns up means read from the bottom upward

parts.note: a lass is a girl
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: A girl arrives with some fibre.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' puts I inside LASS (LASIS) and 'turns up' reverses that.
explanation.definitionFit: Sisal is a stiff plant fibre from an agave, used for rope and matting.

clue.text: Isn't commonly about the East, of course

parts.note: ain't is the common, colloquial form of isn't
re means about, concerning

explanation.surface: Someone talks slangily about the Orient, naturally.
explanation.walkthrough: 'of course' looks like 'naturally' but means a racecourse: Aintree, near Liverpool, hosts the Grand National steeplechase.
explanation.definitionFit: Aintree is the racecourse where the Grand National is run, a racing venue.

clue.text: Still get one pole for the price at 25?

parts.note: still can mean even, as in still more or even more
S is the South Pole

explanation.surface: Get one pole for the price of another, a bargain.
explanation.walkthrough: 'get one' is a link. The definition points to 25 across, AINTREE: evens is a betting price a horse might start at there.
explanation.definitionFit: Evens is betting odds of one to one, a price a bookmaker may offer on a horse.

clue.text: Courses in confectionery

parts.note: a sweet is a pudding course
meat is a main course

explanation.surface: Classes in sweet-making.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Courses' looks like lessons but gives two meal courses, pudding and meat.
explanation.definitionFit: A sweetmeat is an old word for a candy or sugared delicacy.

clue.text: Uninterested in maintaining an even keel

explanation.surface: Someone bored by keeping a boat upright.
explanation.walkthrough: The second definition reads the word as 'list-less': a ship that does not list (lean) stays on an even keel.
explanation.definitionFit: Lacking energy or enthusiasm is apathy, and a vessel without any lean is level.

clue.text: Boxer on the moon ?

parts.note: a boxer can be one who packs things into crates, and the moon's surface is pitted with impact hollows

explanation.surface: A fighter in space.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Boxer' suggests a fighter, but read it as one who puts things in crates; the moon is famous for its pits.
explanation.definitionFit: Lunar hollows made by meteor impacts carry this name, which also reads as a person who packs crates.
